records.text: 86. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the United Nations, the international community and donors: (a) Mobilize additional humanitarian aid and resources to meet the urgent needs of internally displaced persons in Mozambique, including food, shelter, clean water, health care, protection and psychosocial support; (b) Provide support for the establishment and reinforcement of protection mechanisms to ensure the safety and security of internally displaced persons, particularly in conflict-affected areas, including through the deployment of peacekeeping or monitoring missions, when needed; (c) Support the efforts of the Government to address the root causes of conflict in Mozambique through inclusive dialogue, mediation and reconciliation processes involving all relevant stakeholders, including governmental authorities, armed groups and affected communities; (d) Invest in long-term development programmes and resilience-building initiatives to address the underlying drivers of internal displacement, including poverty, inequality, unemployment and lack of access to basic services and livelihood opportunities; (e) Provide technical assistance and capacity-building support to the Government to strengthen its capacity to prevent, respond to and address internal displacement, including through the development of national policies, legal frameworks and coordination mechanisms; (f) Support efforts to enhance data collection and monitoring systems to accurately assess the scale, dynamics and needs of internally displaced populations, including the identification of vulnerable populations and gaps in humanitarian assistance; (g) Ensure the inclusion of host communities in any humanitarian assistance project or development initiative; (h) Promote the engagement of development actors and assist the Government in the implementation of durable solutions, including through sustainable cash-based initiatives, vocational training and income-generating activities.

records.text: 85. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government of Mozambique take the following measures to address issues in the extractive industry: (a) Ensure free, prior and informed consent in extractive projects, allowing affected communities and vulnerable groups to meaningfully participate in decision ‐ making processes that may impact their lands, livelihoods and other rights; (b) Conduct comprehensive human rights impact assessments to minimize negative impacts on affected communities, prevent or reduce displacement, provide adequate compensation and resettlement assistance, when necessary, and safeguard livelihoods and access to essential services; (c) Involve the national bar association and civil society organizations in human rights litigation to ensure direct and quality legal support to resettled communities and empower communities and build their capacity and ensure their meaningful participation and consultation in extractive industry-led projects.

records.text: 84. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government of Mozambique take the following measures to ensure durable solutions: (a) Design protocols, spelling out satisfactory conditions for voluntary return to places of origin, local integration or relocation on a sustainable basis and in circumstances of safety and dignity; such protocols must adhere to human rights principles, ensuring voluntary return in safety and dignity, based on free, informed individual choice, and be implemented and monitored by civilian agencies within the Government; (b) Ensure physical safety in return areas, including by investing in the reconstruction and development of conflict-affected areas to enhance safety, livelihood opportunities and access to basic services; (c) Develop, in consultation with internally displaced persons and the international community, a framework for durable solutions, clarifying the roles and responsibilities of different stakeholders; (d) Facilitate the return of internally displaced persons, when part of an informed and voluntary decision, to their places of origin or integration into new communities; (e) Ensure meaningful participation of displacement-affected communities in the planning and management of durable solutions, with due consideration of vulnerable groups, respecting their dignity, rights and autonomy through, inter alia, strengthening representative forums, consultation mechanisms and community-led initiatives; (f) Empower local communities through recovery and reconstruction efforts and capacity-building and support for community-based organizations and promote the socioeconomic integration of internally displaced persons into host communities or new areas of settlement by facilitating access to essential services and promoting social cohesion; (g) Guarantee the participation of internally displaced persons in planning their return, resettlement or reintegration; (h) Develop a national plan addressing issues related to reparation and justice, ensuring the participation of internally displaced persons and returnees and exploring various forms of reparation (individual, collective, material or symbolic); the plan can be part of a broader transitional justice process that promotes reconciliation and ensures the protection of victims of human rights violations; (i) Expand income-generating schemes to provide internally displaced persons and returnees with dignified livelihood opportunities and promote their self ‐ sufficiency, enabling their participation in economic activities and social security programmes.

records.text: 83. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government of Mozambique take the following measures in the area of protection and access to justice: (a) Ensure the safety and security of internally displaced persons, with special focus on vulnerable groups such as female-headed households and unaccompanied children, older persons and persons with disabilities, including establishing or reinforcing district and provincial-level protection-centred and rights-based mechanisms, committees and community-led structures; (b) Ensure that humanitarian aid reaches all internally displaced persons and host communities when needed, without discrimination based on gender, ethnicity, religion or any other factor and implement robust monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to track the distribution of humanitarian aid and ensure its effectiveness and impartiality; (c) Ensure that internally displaced persons have access to legal and administrative documentation, including simplified procedures for issuing essential documentation and the use of alternative forms of evidence, and reduce administrative requirements and unreasonable conditions; (d) Ensure that internally displaced persons are aware of the free legal and judicial assistance provided by the Institute for Sponsorship and Legal Assistance, strengthen access to justice and awareness-raising campaigns in remote areas and ensure that information about access to justice mechanisms and available services is widely known among internally displaced persons and is free and accessible in their local languages; (e) Take measures to ensure prompt, thorough, independent and impartial investigation of and ensure accountability for human rights violations and abuses committed against internally displaced persons by security forces, community leaders and others with power or involved in humanitarian assistance in order to break the cycle of impunity and fear to denounce cases, strengthen confidential complaint mechanisms and referral pathways to promptly and effectively address complaints and provide necessary support, protection and reparations; (f) Take preventive measures to protect children from grave violations, including abduction and recruitment into armed groups, by enhancing the training of security forces and community awareness; (g) Accelerate efforts to strengthen gender-based violence responses under the auspices of the Ministry of Gender, Children, and Social Action by strengthening and expanding its capacity and institutionalizing integrated survivor-centred services and community-based initiatives, expanding women and girls safe spaces and ensuring accessibility and economic empowerment and ensure dignified reintegration and rehabilitation services and comprehensive protection, reparation, rehabilitation and psychosocial care to survivors of gender-based violence and conflict-related sexual violence to effectively address and respond to their needs and to tackle stigma; (h) Ensure comprehensive sexuality education, prioritizing internally displaced out-of-school adolescents, to tackle teenage pregnancies and child marriage and ensure that community-based legal assistance provides awareness of child marriage issues and that mechanisms are in place to report and promptly respond to suspected or confirmed cases; (i) Provide conditions for community activists to facilitate their transportation to hard-to-reach areas and ensure a coordinated gender-based violence response, including case referral and management under the auspices of the Ministry of Gender, Children, and Social Action; (j) Ensure that gender-based violence prevention awareness campaigns are broadcast on mass media and through community-based initiatives and provide continuous capacity-building and training for service providers, multisectoral coordination and sustainability evaluations for existing centres for assistance and integration; (k) Strengthen community-based mental health and psychosocial services for children and their families in internally displaced persons’ sites and returnee locations through increasing the number of social workers, therapists and psychologists to support communities affected by multiple displacements and extreme violence; (l) Adopt measures to protect housing, land and property rights of internally displaced persons, including preventing unlawful occupation or seizure of land and providing tenure security for housing and land, ensure that fair compensation, resettlement assistance and alternative forms of tenure security are available and sensitize host communities providing land for cultivation by internally displaced persons to mitigate intercommunity land disputes and risks of forced eviction;

records.text: 82. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government of Mozambique take the following measures relative to its legal, policy and institutional framework: (a) Develop and/or strengthen legal and policy frameworks on internal displacement by incorporating the provisions of the Kampala Convention and international and legal standards covering all phases of displacement, including the prohibition of all forms of arbitrary displacement, with a whole-of-government approach to its implementation and clear responsibilities for institutions and effective coordination mechanisms; (b) Incorporate anti-discrimination provisions into the national legislation and enforce measures to protect vulnerable groups of internally displaced persons; (c) Clarify the responsibilities and competences of the National Institute of Disaster Management in order to adjust its capacity to carry out its newly mandated coordinating activities, aimed at protecting and assisting internally displaced persons in the context of disasters, armed conflict and violence; (d) Expedite the approval of the law on promotion and protection of the rights of persons with disabilities in line with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and implement international guidelines for the inclusion of disabilities in humanitarian action; (e) Finalize the revision of the 1997 land law to improve land tenure and access to housing, land and property rights, emphasizing community participation, non ‐ discrimination and gender equality in land access, and establish procedures for the restitution or compensation of land and property rights for internally displaced persons upon their return or resettlement; (f) Adopt a comprehensive legal and policy framework to address the situation of survivors of conflict-related sexual violence, many of whom remain in displacement, including by providing reparation through a comprehensive, inclusive and survivor-centred programme; (g) Strengthen the capacity of governmental institutions to effectively address the rights and needs of internally displaced persons, especially the most vulnerable, through training, resource allocation and improved coordination mechanisms; (h) Strengthen the leadership and ownership of local, administrative and provincial authorities, clarifying their roles in supporting internal displacement within the national policy framework and ensuring decentralization and localization of displacement responses, as well as coordination and oversight; (i) Ensure that the National Human Rights Commission is aligned with the principles relating to the status of national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights (Paris Principles) and has the necessary resources to effectively fulfil its mandate, including on the promotion and protection of the rights of internally displaced persons; (j) Strengthen legal and regulatory frameworks governing the extractive industry to ensure that they adequately protect the rights of affected communities, including provisions related to land rights, compensation and resettlement; (k) Strengthen data collection mechanisms on internal displacement with clearly designated responsibilities to collect, analyse and disseminate a consolidated and disaggregated data on internal displacement.

records.text: 81. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government of Mozambique: (a) Ensure the protection and safety of internally displaced persons, particularly in conflict-affected areas, and ensure human rights monitoring and unimpeded humanitarian access and take proactive measures to prevent forced displacement by addressing root causes of conflict, promoting dialogue, mediation and ensuring compliance with international human rights and humanitarian law; (b) Ensure a protection-centred and inclusive response to the conflict and natural disasters affecting vulnerable populations, including during displacement, return and relocation, including actively engaging and involving all affected population groups in shaping the response in order to mitigate protection risks and meet basic needs, such as housing, food, water, medical services and sanitation; (c) Strengthen disaster preparedness and response to mitigate the impact of natural disasters on internal displacement through the effective implementation of the National Disaster Risk Reduction Master Plan 2017–2030, enhancing national and local capacities, as well as coordination among line ministries at the national and provincial level and collaborating with relevant stakeholders, including civil society organizations and affected communities, to ensure their meaningful consultation and the timely dissemination of information; (d) Ensure that the sectoral interventions in the disaster risk reduction and management cycle for the national contingency plan include dedicated resources for internally displaced persons and host communities; (e) Revisit the process and the scope of stakeholder engagement to enable a comprehensive approach to solutions under the national policy and strategy for internal displacement management; (f) Provide training and capacity-building activities to defence and security forces on standards relating to human rights and international humanitarian law and strengthen the capacity of relevant governmental bodies to effectively prevent, respond and address internal displacement; (g) Continue efforts to adopt a comprehensive national action plan on business and human rights, in line with the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, including monitoring, reporting and enforcement mechanisms to track the impact of extractive activities on internal displacement and to hold extractive companies and relevant stakeholders accountable.

records.text: 76. The Special Rapporteur commends the Government for the remarkable progress made in responding to a complex displacement situation driven both by conflict and disasters and the adverse effects of climate change that resulted in over 1.2 million internally displaced persons and an additional 110,000 internally displaced persons following the early 2024 attacks in the north. More than 600,000 people returned to their areas of origin in 2023. However, important challenges persist, both for the remaining displaced population, as well as for those who have returned. The Government must continue to support durable solutions, enhanced and cohesive measures, justice and reparation, with the participation of internally displaced persons. 77. The invitation extended to the Special Rapporteur by the Government and its willingness to engage with her mandate is a testament to its political will to address displacement issues. The commitment shown by Mozambique to the Secretary ‐ General’s Action Agenda on Internal Displacement is a significant step towards ensuring durable solutions for internally displaced persons. More concerted efforts are needed to address the remaining challenges and to develop a strategy for the comprehensive protection of and assistance to internally displaced persons. 78. Ahead of the upcoming elections in October 2024, against the backdrop of a fragile security situation, there is momentum to accelerate the commitment of the Government to maintain the issue on the agenda, to expedite its responses and to scale up livelihoods and resilience-building activities, as well as development and local integration related interventions in the central and northern part of the country, ensuring that the critical needs of the population are adequately addressed. There is a need for a common long-term vision, funding and a road map, based on the Inter ‐ Agency Standing Committee Framework on Durable Solutions for Internally Displaced Persons, for humanitarian, peace and development actors to commit to in addressing internal displacement, with clear responsibilities, tasks, timelines and financial allocations under the leadership and coordination of the Government . 79. The Resident Coordinator, on behalf of the United Nations country team and the durable solutions working group, should work with the Government to support efforts to seek early solutions, emphasizing they must be voluntary and safe. Key policies should be identified and incentives put in place in order that solutions may be approved in a timely manner. 80. Informed by the Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement and the Inter ‐ Agency Standing Committee Framework on Durable Solutions for Internally Displaced Persons, the Special Rapporteur makes the following recommendations.

records.section: Protection risks faced by internally displaced persons in Mozambique
records.text: 70. In line with the 2010 Inter-Agency Standing Committee Framework on Durable Solutions for Internally Displaced Persons, achieving durable solutions means that internally displaced persons no longer have displacement-specific needs and can enjoy their rights without discrimination. The primary responsibility for facilitating voluntary, safe and dignified return or resettlement lies with the State, with the active participation of internally displaced persons. Mozambique faces both promising prospects and significant challenges in achieving durable solutions in this regard. 71. The fluid nature of patterns of return pose significant concerns, with returnees facing precarious conditions, including limited access to health care, livelihoods, education and security. There is a lack of proper planning, consultation and coordination, compromising informed decision-making by and the safety and well-being of internally displaced persons in areas of return. Local authorities and community leaders sometimes exert indirect pressure on internally displaced persons to return by promising assistance or providing incomplete information about living conditions. Many internally displaced persons have had to settle in villages or district capitals near rather than in their places of origin as a result of the destruction of housing and security issues. Oftentimes, internally displaced persons must stay in makeshift accommodations such as schools and other temporary evacuation sites, with inadequate facilities and heightened risks of gender-based violence. Some returns facilitated by the military risked contravening humanitarian principles and posed security risks. Other challenges to the sustainability of returns included discrimination, limited livelihood opportunities, food insecurity, insecure land tenure rights and volatile security situations. Limited livelihoods and disrupted services contributed to family separation and the frequent need to move between areas of return and displacement sites, as well as between urban and rural areas, to access services and livelihoods. 72. The ability of the Government to ensure minimum conditions for return were hampered by its impaired capacity to deliver public services owing to the impact of the movements of displaced persons on civil service personnel and infrastructure, particularly in conflict-affected areas. Such protection gaps posed significant challenges. 73. Efforts to enhance coordination across the humanitarian-development-peace nexus continue, yet challenges persist owing to the absence of a coordinated platform for addressing internal displacement. It is crucial to align durable solutions, reconstruction, development and stabilization initiatives under a Government-led consolidated strategic approach, integrating human rights, humanitarian, development and peace efforts. Humanitarian actors, who play a key role in enabling solutions, must prioritize planning for solutions from the outset. The Government is urged to tackle existing obstacles hindering durable solutions and to devise a clear, human rights-based plan aligned with international standards, specifying what durable solutions entail and how their achievement will be measured and verified. 74. The Special Rapporteur recalls that durable solutions require multidisciplinary, whole-of-government and community-driven programmes, sustained commitment, collaboration and resource mobilization. Development investments for internally displaced persons should be complementary, so as to increase resilience, rather than coming at the expense of protection, humanitarian and other forms of assistance. Protection measures should be integrated throughout all stages of humanitarian action in order to address and mitigate protection needs effectively. This includes strengthening the presence and the technical and institutional capacity and outreach of key agencies, including the National Institute of Disaster Management, the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Action and the National Commission of Human Rights, in all provinces and districts and fostering a protection-centred, inclusive and sustainable humanitarian response during rapid onset emergencies. While the Government has shifted the focus from a purely humanitarian response to more sustainable approaches, the current situation in Cabo Delgado remains dynamic and protection needs acute, meaning that life-saving assistance will remain pertinent in secure areas, while others may benefit from longer term development and local integration processes. Addressing the underlying drivers of displacement, strengthening protection mechanisms, both for internally displaced persons and returnees, and promoting social cohesion and inclusive development, both for internally displaced persons and host communities, are essential in order to foster lasting solutions. 75. The meaningful and inclusive participation of internally displaced persons and host communities in decisions affecting them, including in the design of policies aimed at meeting their assistance and protection needs, supporting returns and other forms of durable solutions, as well as in processes to ensure accountability for violations committed, is essential to ensure their sustainability, relevance and ownership both by internally displaced persons and host communities. The upcoming elections present an opportunity for the genuine and full political participation of internally displaced persons and returnees, fostering their sustainable reintegration into the political, economic and social life of Mozambique.

records.text: 63. Amid the significant displacement crisis, the international community has provided crucial humanitarian assistance to those in need by delivering lifesaving protection services, livelihood and income-generating activities and economic empowerment to internally displaced persons. In 2023, 1.6 million people in northern Mozambique received some form of aid, including food assistance, reaching 1.4 million individuals. However, declining funding limited their ability to provide comprehensive assistance, leaving many with unmet needs in critical areas like nutrition, education and protection. As a result, humanitarian actors were forced to make difficult choices, such as curtailing food rations to cover a larger caseload of beneficiaries and stretching the provision of services between displaced people and returning internally displaced persons, affecting the quality of aid and increasing protection risks. 64. In 2024, humanitarian efforts target 1.7 million people, including those affected by conflict and natural disasters. Anticipatory action initiatives aim to mitigate the impact of natural disasters on an estimated 2.5 million vulnerable individuals. 65. On numerous occasions the Special Rapporteur heard about the need for better coordination of activities between key humanitarian and development actors and about somewhat fragmented efforts across different donors, agencies and locations in the humanitarian aid response, including lack of coherence between humanitarian assistance and recovery efforts and lingering bureaucratic hurdles delaying the delivery of grants. 66. The Special Rapporteur welcomes the country’s Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan 2024, which outlines a framework for collaboration with the Government, development actors and the private sector to rebuild infrastructure and essential services. Furthermore, the humanitarian country team protection strategy 2023–2025 guides the humanitarian community in addressing critical protection risks faced by affected population and integrating protection into all aspects of the humanitarian response. The strategy aims to prevent, reduce and respond to protection risks in conflict and natural disaster scenarios, focusing on upholding children’s rights, supporting survivors of gender-based violence and enhancing the capacity of the Government in disaster-prone areas. It aligns with the Secretary-General’s call to action for human rights to ensure that affected persons can enjoy their rights, rebuild their lives and achieve sustainable solutions in dignity and safety. 67. Limited information exchanges between humanitarian and development structures on recovery, stabilization and development and social cohesion results and absence of an overview of the nexus spectrum, underscoring the need for high-quality disaggregated data and community involvement in decision-making. The Government has established the Mozambique Information System to track interventions in the north with a potential to broaden its scope, with a few partners sharing information on ongoing efforts. There is a continued need for high-quality disaggregated data and analysis for evidence-based interventions and for consultations with and the involvement of internally displaced persons and host communities in decisions affecting them. 68. While recognizing the need for continued humanitarian support to internally displaced persons in Mozambique and for shifting the balance to engage with development, peace and disaster management, it is necessary to tackle the governance, infrastructure, social cohesion, security and risk reduction components that are essential for achieving durable solutions at scale. The Special Rapporteur called upon the Government and key humanitarian, development and peace actors to accelerate efforts to develop a State-owned and driven human rights-based plan and protection strategy, focusing on the meaning of human rights‐based and driven durable solutions and on how the Government would measure and verify such solutions when they are achieved. 69. Addressing the significant funding shortfall is paramount in order to meet the protection needs of internally displaced persons. The humanitarian response in northern Mozambique remains severely underfunded. An estimated 2.25 million people require humanitarian assistance and protection, including 1.7 million people affected by conflict in northern Mozambique and 554,000 people impacted by natural hazards during the rainy/cyclonic season. The Special Rapporteur called upon the international and donor community to support to the Mozambique Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan for 2024, which requires $413 million to address urgent needs arising from multiple crises in the country.

records.section: Protection risks faced by internally displaced persons in Mozambique
records.text: 40. Internally displaced persons affected by natural disasters face numerous challenges, including: breakdown of social structures; lack of livelihood opportunities; lack of health care; equal access to education; lack of sanitation; food security; inadequate housing; lack of privacy; gender-based violence; loss of documentation; lack of equal and inclusive access to assistance; unsafe or involuntary return or resettlement; and property restitution issues. Protection risks are especially high for women and girls, older people and people with disabilities, with women and girls experiencing a higher risk of gender-based violence owing to their caregiving responsibilities, increased exposure in remote areas to check on their households and plots of land (machambas) and to access essential services such as water, medical facilities, markets or farms, in addition to structural inequalities and gender norms in the community. 41. Relocation and transit centres lacked feedback and accessible complaint mechanisms for reporting allegations of gender-based violence, leading to a significant underreporting of such cases. Contributing factors include reluctance to disclose incidents and the withdrawal of complaints as a result of family pressure and stigma. Additionally, there is a lack of awareness among internally displaced persons regarding their rights and their entitlement to protection. This lack of awareness is compounded by a lack of trust and fear of reprisals, exacerbated by fatigue resulting from repeated visits and interviews by various actors. In some interactions, there is insufficient consideration of the “do no harm” principle; such interactions often fail to yield tangible outcomes or to effect improvement in their lives. 42. The Special Rapporteur was informed about the suspension of pensions and social welfare subsidies for persons with disabilities and older persons, their sole sources of income, lasting for several months. Persons with disabilities, who may lack caregivers, were at higher risk of experiencing violence, exploitation and abuse. Further, many of their assistive devices were outdated or not tailored to individual needs. The temporary learning centres in some relocation sites needed reconstruction. 43. Initial humanitarian responses to internal displacement have mainly focused on accommodation centres, with poor or delayed interventions for vulnerable groups who were unable to access them owing to distance or lack of information. Internally displaced persons are routinely exposed to sexual exploitation and abuse, including requests for sexual favours during the establishment of beneficiary lists and the provision of humanitarian assistance. Others resort to “survival sex” to obtain basic needs. Temporary shelters and accommodations lacked complaint mechanisms and information on how to report cases. Many internally displaced persons mentioned the lack of timely, inclusive, accessible and accurate information about resettlement sites and information on their choice of resettlement locations. 44. The Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Welfare, the primary government body responsible for the protection of vulnerable groups, faces significant challenges in promptly addressing protection concerns and delivering emergency assistance, in coordination with authorities at the provincial, district and community levels. Despite having nominal presence in provinces and districts, its institutional capacity and resources were severely strained. The Ministry also faces challenges in coordinating emergency responses, including resource allocation, information dissemination, outreach efforts and distribution of kits deployed by other governmental agencies, NGOs and humanitarian organizations. In addition, the Ministry lacks specialized institutional capacity to offer psychosocial support in cases of severe trauma suffered by internally displaced persons. 45. The displacement crisis in Cabo Delgado has led to severe loss of livelihoods and heightened vulnerability among civilians, exacerbated by an underfunded humanitarian response. Food insecurity and protection from gender-based violence were particularly acute among internally displaced populations, disproportionately affecting women and girls, children, persons with disabilities and older persons. According to the United Nations Humanitarian Protection Strategy 2023, about 15 per cent of the displaced population is composed of individuals with disabilities, who face heightened risks of gender-based violence owing to inadequate planning at internally displaced persons’ sites and limited access to essential services. Serious protection risks, combined with the limited capacity of the Government and humanitarian actors, have strained the coping abilities of the displaced population and increased its vulnerability. 46. At the time of her visit, despite the heavy footprint of international humanitarian actors in the north, the overall protection environment in Cabo Delgado remained fluid and dynamic, requiring continuous assessment and analysis to inform humanitarian responses, including challenges posed by lack of security and poor infrastructure in hard-to-reach areas. 47. The recent escalation in internal displacement has raised significant human rights concerns, including on missing and unaccompanied children, forced recruitment into armed groups and sexual violence. 48. The security situation has impeded the efforts of protection partners to assist affected communities, disrupting community support structures and hindering access to services. At the time of the visit, humanitarian assistance and protection measures were insufficient to meet the needs of those who have lost homes and property, with no assistance for housing access or legal reparations. In addition there was an acute need for mental health and psychosocial support services, in particular among children, who have been victims of grave human rights violations and who lack specialized services for their rescue, release and reintegration into communities. 49. There are ongoing efforts by key governmental agencies to assist affected communities, albeit fragmented and with limited technical capacity and outreach, including lack of fuel for local operations. Interventions by Government, development and protection actors are often project based and may lack sustainability in the longer term. 50. While primary protection needs in both current displacement and return areas include civil documentation, child protection, legal assistance, physical safety and security, protection from gender-based violence (including risks associated with survival sex and early and forced marriage) and mental health and psychosocial support services, there is also a need to strengthen the integration and mainstreaming of human rights protection considerations in key sectors, such as food security and livelihoods, health care, shelter and water, sanitation and hygiene. 51. The Special Rapporteur hopes that the Government’s annual contingency plan and the 2024 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan for Mozambique will alleviate protection risks and concerns, strengthen livelihoods and enhance resilience. The plans aim to provide protection and assistance, including food aid, non-food items and dignity kits, with a particular focus on addressing the protection needs of women and girls. 52. Access to justice for internally displaced persons, including legal aid for critical protection services like gender-based violence, has been severely limited. Existing disparities in access to legal aid, fear of retaliation when reporting or denouncing cases, lengthy judicial processes and lack of prompt investigation have exacerbated feelings of injustice and mistrust in the administration of justice. In response, community and informal justice mechanisms have been reinstated at internally displaced persons’ sites. However, such mechanisms lack due process and cannot fully replace formal justice systems, particularly regarding serious human rights violations, such as gender-based violence. 53. Capacity-building for judiciary, law enforcement, community and local administration personnel on the human rights of internally displaced persons is crucial, as is the provision of training and resources for entities offering legal aid and expertise to deal with cases arising from land issues in both resettlement and host communities. Strengthening justice institutions is vital in rebuilding public trust. The Special Rapporteur welcomes the “One district, One court” initiative and believes that consolidating justice services, such as the halls of justice (palácios de justiçia) initiative, could further improve the accessibility and effectiveness of the administration of justice. 54. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur learned that some perceived or actual members of non-State armed groups had surrendered their weapons following a Presidential pardon in September 2023, with assurances of pardon and reintegration into their communities. She heard concerns regarding the fear and retraumatization of victims and survivors of human rights violations committed by members of former non-State armed groups upon their reintegration into communities. Transparent and inclusive transitional justice measures are urgently needed, involving community discussions to promote social cohesion and reconciliation and to ensure the protection of victims’ human rights, including truth, justice, reparation, rehabilitation and non-recurrence guarantees. 55. During discussions with internally displaced persons, accessibility to civil documentation emerged as a critical concern. Lack of documentation exposes internally displaced persons to protection risks, including restricted movement, gender-based violence and denial of services. Efforts to provide documentation, including through establishing mobile brigades, while ongoing were not universally accessible, leading to delays and the increased vulnerability of internally displaced persons. 56. The lack of civil documentation and the destruction of infrastructure present challenges to internally displaced persons seeking access to housing and land and property rights in both displacement and resource-rich areas of return, leading to instances of forced evictions, illegal expropriations, illegal occupations and land disputes. In areas of ongoing armed clashes, many returnees are unable to resume their livelihoods owing to insecurity in accessing their farmland or obtaining their housing and lands, including in areas where existing forms of tenure security existed. As a result, internally displaced persons may need to engage in intercommunity land disputes in their places of origin, exposing them to further risk of forced eviction and thereby jeopardizing their sustainable return and reintegration. In urban areas, displaced individuals face high housing prices and threats of eviction. Despite the country’s land-tenure framework guaranteeing equal rights, ineffective enforcement and discriminatory norms have marginalized women. 57. Internally displaced children have endured violence, exploitation, forced marriage and recruitment into armed groups, leaving them traumatized and in dire need of mental health and psychosocial support. Many protection actors pointed out to the high rate of child prostitution in Pemba city, including among the displaced population, and the lack of protection services available to them. Children who escaped from non-State armed groups have suffered atrocities and faced discrimination and stigmatization upon release. The Special Rapporteur welcomed the procedures developed by the Ministry of National Defence for caring for children in armed conflict and urged the Government to endorse the Principles and Guidelines on Children Associated with Armed Forces or Armed Groups, to continue training its security forces on the prevention of grave violations against children and establishing child protection focal points. Children allegedly associated with non-State armed groups should not face arrest and prosecution solely for their membership in such groups. Comprehensive child protection measures should be put in place, including specialized support for their rescue and for their physical and psychological recovery and social reintegration. 58. Strengthening community-based mental health and psychosocial services, including specialized support for children and families, is crucial. Increased availability of social workers, therapists and psychologists is necessary to address the acute needs in communities affected by displacement and violence. The Special Rapporteur was encouraged by the adoption of a victim-centred approach by key protection actors, prioritizing the do not harm principle and victims’ safety, rights, well-being and choices. 59. The Special Rapporteur called for targeted awareness-raising campaigns on existing laws criminalizing child marriage, the protection of whistle-blowers and accelerated efforts to deliver comprehensive sexuality education, especially targeting out-of-school adolescents, including internally displaced persons, in order to address inequalities and harmful practices such as child marriage, teenage pregnancy, gender-based violence and sexual and reproductive health issues. 60. The Special Rapporteur heard about numerous allegations of non-consensual relationships and rape by non-State armed groups and security forces. Survivors, particularly women and girls released from captivity, face revictimization and stigma and often relocate owing to fear of encountering their perpetrators. The victims suffer from poverty, stigma, unwanted pregnancies, sexual and reproductive health issues, document loss and lack of safe housing. Insufficient housing and barriers to accessing services for gender-based violence exacerbate their plight, compounded by fear of discrimination and limited awareness of available support. Gender-based violence services provided by the State, already limited, have been further disrupted by conflict and displacement and lack comprehensive victim‐centric programmes. Establishing or strengthening mechanisms to support survivors, including medical care, psychosocial support and safe shelter, is crucial for the reintegration of internally displaced persons into communities. Pathways providing access to justice for all survivors of gender-based violence must be strengthened and perpetrators held accountable. Mandatory and continuous training on gender-based violence for all security forces, along with transparent measures for internal oversight and accountability, are crucial. The Special Rapporteur commended the Government for planning to expand the integrated centres for assistance and reintegration, which survivors value for their services and local coordination. Such centres should be established nationwide and reinforced with trained staff and multisectoral coordination. Enhancing survivor-centred case management is crucial, including comprehensive health care, legal, mental health and security services. The prevention of gender-based violence requires extensive awareness campaigns on mass media and through community initiatives, expanding safe spaces for women and girls and prioritizing the distribution of dignity kits and support vouchers. 61. The Special Rapporteur learned of numerous instances where women and girls engaged in survival sex in exchange for food or humanitarian aid, including with community representatives who act on behalf of authorities and are responsible, inter alia, for tracking the displacement and movement of affected populations and drawing up lists of beneficiaries for assistance. Women and girls have repeatedly stressed their need to feel safe and free of fear to report allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse by individuals in power. While the overall security situation at internally displaced persons’ sites has improved owing to the deployment of police, such measures are no substitute for confidential reporting and complaint mechanisms. The latter are often perceived as less efficient due to delays in processing complaints. The recently approved code of conduct for humanitarian actors adopted by the National Institute of Disaster Management, which applies to all humanitarian actors and community leaders involved in humanitarian assistance, should be strictly implemented. Strengthening accountability mechanisms associated with the code is essential in order to ensure proper reporting and response and the protection of whistle‐blowers. 62. Urgent attention needs to be paid to the situation of internally displaced persons with disabilities and persons with diverse sexual orientation and gender identity, who encounter stigma, discrimination and obstacles in accessing essential services. Disability-inclusive emergency response plans and policies are essential to address their specific needs during the disaster management cycle and to enable meaningful participation. To improve dignity and protection for individuals with disabilities, it is critical to prioritize the provision of assistive devices and to ensure inclusive, accessible and non-discriminatory services. Authorities should establish disability-inclusive disaster preparedness and recovery guidelines, in consultation with disability-related organizations by accelerating the approval of the pending disability law, in line with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

records.text: 24. The Government of Mozambique has made important strides in addressing the challenges posed by internal displacement. The Special Rapporteur commended the Government for its early action and prompt response to Tropical Cyclone Freddy in 2023, including the establishment of accommodation centres across Sofala Province and the delivery of a wide range of services. While similar efforts were made in response to Cyclone Idai in 2019, they were impeded by limited human and financial resources, significant infrastructure gaps and regional disparities across the country. The central and northern regions of the country – the areas with the highest poverty rates – received the lowest levels of assistance and coverage, exacerbated by the aftermath of conflicts and natural disasters. 25. At the time of her visit, the Special Rapporteur was informed by the Government that out of 181,660 internally displaced persons in central and southern Mozambique, 130,000 were in a situation of protracted displacement. The transition to recovery seems to have been deprioritized in view of the crises in the north, resulting in people living in resettlement sites for years with limited livelihood opportunities, insecure land tenure and insufficient access to adequate housing. In some resettlement sites that were initially meant to be transitional and short-term, internally displaced persons lacked livelihood opportunities and subsistence agricultural lands to sustain their families. 26. Displacement caused by natural hazards and climate shocks exacerbates vulnerability, with recurrent shocks hindering recovery and resilience-building efforts. Relocations often lack sufficient investment in infrastructure and services, leaving displaced populations in vulnerable conditions. While some resettlement areas, such as Guara Guara, hosting over 25,000 internally displaced persons, have seen improvements in infrastructure, albeit slow, including a new hospital and expanded water system coverage, overall living conditions remain precarious. The internally displaced persons the Special Rapporteur met with lacked access to basic necessities like food, health care, water, education and housing. The construction of a new school has been pending completion for the past five years. 27. Internally displaced persons stressed the importance of income-generating initiatives and projects led, inter alia, by the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Action in achieving self-sufficiency and reducing dependency on cash-based transfers. The Ministry was planning to graduate over 120,000 beneficiaries enrolled in revenue-generating initiatives. Between 2024 and 2026, 110 households will take part in capacity-building activities, followed by subsidies, management training and access to savings and revolving funds to support livelihood sustainability. Internally displaced persons stressed the importance of ensuring that such initiatives are also made accessible to their host communities and recommended that the Government finds ways to address discrepancies and perceptions of discrimination within those communities to make sure that efforts to construct facilities and infrastructure in resettlement sites do not disregard the needs and concerns of host communities, thereby prompting tensions. 28. Food security was significantly compromised in the areas visited, especially for vulnerable groups, including children, older persons and persons with disabilities owing to a lack of clarity about the frequency of food distribution by humanitarian actors; in the absence of livelihood opportunities, such distributions were the only source of food for many displaced populations. The quality of services provided in camps varied significantly; camps were managed by different organizations or operated by ad hoc projects overseen by international organizations and their sustainability was uncertain. Emergency shelters in some camps urgently required renovation, especially in camps with long-term displaced populations who were still unable to return to their areas of origin. Many internally displaced persons and returnees who have experienced traumatic events required specialized mental health and psychosocial support services, which were mostly absent. 29. Displacement in the context of disasters and climate change is a recurring challenge in Mozambique. Many people continue to live in high-risk areas owing to a range of factors, including affordability and the availability of services and livelihood opportunities. However, living in such areas perpetuates a cycle of recurrent shocks and displacements, hindering recovery and resilience-building efforts for internally displaced persons. Displacement following disasters and climate-related shocks is typically perceived as temporary. The movement of internally displaced persons to relocation sites does not always include a guarantee of access to basic services at the sites or in nearby urban settlements. There is no comprehensive relocation plan ensuring that relocations are carried out, from the start, in line with protection standards and principles, including a durable solutions perspective in order to avoid secondary displacement and the creation of new humanitarian needs. 30. Disasters are a persistent reality in Mozambique and there is an urgent need to bolster the resilience of existing settlements. Mitigation, adaptation and other feasible measures to avoid displacement should be explored and exhausted. Only then may planned relocations be considered as a measure of last resort. It is critical that such relocations respect the rights of affected communities, including internally displaced persons and host communities, as well as the right of internally displaced persons to choose where to settle and find durable solutions to their situation, in line with their preferences, while ensuring their active, meaningful and informed participation in the decision-making process. 31. In ongoing post-cyclone recovery efforts, there is a critical need to expedite the reconstruction of resilient infrastructure and expand services, development and stabilization initiatives in relocation areas, with the active involvement of affected communities in disaster preparedness, humanitarian response and post-disaster recovery. Such efforts must be institutionalized to ensure their sustainability and effectiveness. 32. In northern Mozambique, the humanitarian response is transitioning towards reconstruction, necessitating a comprehensive approach that integrates humanitarian, development and peacebuilding efforts. This requires addressing critical protection and humanitarian needs in conflict-affected and underserved areas, as well as in designated displacement sites. Despite the protracted nature of displacement in Cabo Delgado, many internally displaced persons still rely heavily on humanitarian aid owing to lack of livelihood opportunities, including land for subsistence agriculture. Ongoing humanitarian assistance remains crucial while efforts to enhance self-reliance and resilience are expanded in both displacement and return areas. 33. A comprehensive national response to internal displacement in Mozambique requires adequate allocation of human and financial resources tailored to the protection and assistance needs of internally displaced persons, including streamlined coordination, strengthened institutional capacities and inclusive engagement with national and international stakeholders to achieve durable solutions. While the policy and implementing strategy identifies the roles of local and district authorities in planning and implementing activities for internally displaced persons and in supporting durable solutions, coordination arrangements remain somewhat undefined in practice. Improved coordination among subnational authorities, non‐governmental organizations (NGOs) and international organizations is crucial for enhancing the overall effectiveness of the response. 34. Although existing frameworks contain provisions for resource allocation, there is a need to ensure that resources are earmarked to address both short-term humanitarian needs and long-term solutions. There is also a need for clarity about resource distribution at the national and subnational levels, as well as stronger coordination between the Government and the international community, especially for durable solutions. Integrating displacement issues into national development instruments, such as the revised National Development Strategy 2015–2035, can facilitate strategic resource allocation. 35. While the policy and implementing strategy emphasizes environmental education, risk management and community sensitization, specific measures targeting the general public and relevant stakeholders, including internally displaced persons themselves, are needed to ensure a more inclusive and effective response. 36. To effectively address the needs of displaced populations across different stages of displacement, it is essential to ensure Government-led, locally owned, decentralized interventions that consider the vulnerabilities and protection needs of affected populations. This entails strengthening the leadership and ownership of local, administrative and provincial authorities, clarifying their roles in supporting internal displacement within the national policy framework and ensuring the decentralization and localization of displacement responses. 37. Although various governmental mechanisms for coordination at provincial level are in place, their level of engagement varies, with overlapping responsibilities and duplicative roles. There is a need to enhance clarity and visibility of the coordination mechanisms at the provincial level, particularly in the context of the current crisis in the north and in post‐disaster recovery efforts in cyclone-affected regions. The “programme for resilience and integrated development of the north” was adopted following the recovery and peacebuilding assessment in 2021, with a wider approach to recovery, focusing on the three northern provinces of Cabo Delgado, Nampula and Niassa. This programme can play a crucial role in guiding development and resilience-building efforts that should align with broader national development strategies. There is also a greater need for clarity and visibility at the local level as to the agency leading the interministerial response to current crisis both for the conflict in the north, and for post-disaster recovery for the cyclone-affected regions. A whole of society approach with a clear role of the private sector can be critical to enhance durable solutions supporting livelihoods and promoting sustainable development. 38. Overall, addressing internal displacement in Mozambique requires sustained investment in infrastructure, services, and livelihood opportunities, both for internally displaced persons and host communities, as well as strengthened coordination between Government, NGOs, humanitarian actors and the private sector. The National Human Rights Commission, which has an important role in upholding human rights standards and ensuring accountability, should have the necessary resources and autonomy to effectively fulfil its mandate nationwide, including on the promotion and protection of the rights of internally displaced persons. 39. Despite ongoing data collection efforts for early warning and evacuation planning, systematic updates are lacking during preparedness phases to ensure accuracy in all stages of response and that responses are tailored to protection needs during disasters. There is also a need to collect, analyse and disseminate disaggregated data on internal displacement to ensure better planning, to devise solutions and to track progress collectively and transparently.

records.section: Domestic legal, policy and institutional framework
records.text: 12. Mozambique has made significant progress in addressing internal displacement through legal, policy and institutional frameworks. Efforts have been made to incorporate the Kampala Convention into domestic legislation, enhance disaster risk management and establish policies for internal displacement management, although the dissemination and enforcement of such measures remains low. The existing legal framework lacks provisions against arbitrary displacement and protections during displacement, return and local integration. More efforts could be made to coordinate and clarify roles and responsibilities in order to advance protection and solutions. 13. Mozambique has incorporated the Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement into its legislation and policies. The 10/2020 Law on Disaster Risk Management and Reduction established the National Institute for Disaster Management, which has outlined post-disaster recovery strategies. The above-mentioned law provides the legal framework for disaster risk management, including the prevention and mitigation of the destructive effects of disasters, relief efforts and reconstruction actions. By decree 76/2020, the Government approved regulations for disaster risk reduction and, in resolution 42/2021, approved the national policy and strategy for internal displacement management. The latter is led by the National Institute for Disaster Management as the national focal point coordinating multisectoral interventions across the disaster management cycle, covering both armed conflicts and natural disasters. This comprehensive framework, a response to the crisis in Cabo Delgado, outlines Government’s actions to prevent, assist and reintegrate affected populations, covering both conflict and climate-induced displacement and focusing on durable solutions for displaced individuals. Accompanied by a three-year action plan, it includes capacity-building initiatives, the enhancement of early warning system and the adoption of resilient shelter models. 14. The 2021 policy and implementing strategy on the management of displaced people applies to individuals or groups forced to leave their habitual residences owing to armed conflicts, generalized violence, human rights violations, natural disasters or man-made disasters. While it emphasizes the needs of groups in vulnerable situations, it fails to incorporate anti-discrimination provisions based on displacement, thereby potentially exposing non-national internally displaced persons, habitual residents of diverse nationalities and stateless individuals to the risk of discrimination as constitutional rights are not automatically extended to foreign nationals. 15. The policy and implementing strategy, which lacks a direct prohibition on arbitrary displacement, outlines measures to prevent and manage disaster displacement, such as community resilience-building and preparedness strategies. While it recognizes the movements of internally displaced persons, it does not explicitly address their right to freely move within the country, suggesting that, during the response phase, Mozambican armed forces should adopt mechanisms to “control” such movements without elaborating conditions or mechanisms through which the armed forces could control freedom of movement. While recognizing the significance of assessing the expectations and intentions of internally displaced persons with regard to return, the policy and implementing strategy fails to explicitly recognize their inherent right to make informed and voluntary choices. Furthermore, it overlooks the importance of understanding their preferences, needs and capacities, all of which are fundamental in formulating effective strategies to assist them in rebuilding their lives and achieving durable solutions. 16. The National Disaster Risk Reduction Master Plan 2017–2030, the primary framework for disaster risk management, is aimed at enhancing the country’s resilience through prevention, preparedness, response and recovery measures, with special protections afforded to vulnerable groups during evacuation and resettlement. 17. Although the electoral law allows exceptions to the rule of voting by proxy, the exceptions do not address situations of internal displacement. Further, the policy and implementing strategy lacks specific provisions concerning the participatory rights of internally displaced persons. 18. The Land Act No. 19/1997 regulates land access, use and exploitation rights (duat) and allows for the legalization of customary land rights. If discriminatory customary practices conflict with the Constitution, the latter prevails. Despite constitutional and legal guarantees of gender equality and non-discrimination, women in Mozambique often face insecure land rights. Oversight of customary authorities is lacking and many women in rural areas are unaware of their rights or of legal avenues for enforcement. Although the duat for housing or family use is not limited by time, many Mozambicans reside in informal urban or rural settlements without registration, without protection of their land and housing rights. This leads to significant insecurity in land tenure as informal housing lacks formal legal recognition. Furthermore, the duat acquisition process, as outlined in the Land Act, is both expensive and time-consuming. 19. Although resolution 19/2011 mandates the establishment of disaster insurance mechanisms and the national housing policy and Law No. 10/2020 provide asset protections for citizens evacuated during natural disasters, such protections do not extend to people displaced by armed conflicts. While the legislation focuses on disaster risk reduction and management, it does not specifically prioritize the protection and assistance of internally displaced people regarding the recognition of land rights or restitution. The policy and implementing strategy assigns responsibility to the National Institute of Disaster Management, the Ministry of Land and Environment and the Ministry of Public Works, Housing and Water Resources for shelter and housing needs during recovery, but there is ambiguity regarding their roles, as the three entities are also responsible for settlement and reconstruction in affected areas. 20. Under the policy and implementing strategy, land tenure security for displaced persons is outlined as a strategic action, however, during the response phase, it lacks specifics on how land tenure security will be ensured for internally displaced persons in practice, including mechanisms for recognizing and protecting property rights to abandoned land and providing restitution or compensation in cases of displacement. While the Mozambican real estate registry office safeguards property rights by recording ownership and real estate transactions it also lacks specific provisions to address situations arising from internal displacement. 21. The legal framework provides indemnification and compensation for forced resettlement and land expropriation resulting from national interest projects, including through the 2012 regulation regarding resettlement owing to economic activities, which offers protections and safeguards to affected communities. This is a welcome move, although further improvements will be needed to regulate land access, livelihoods, health care and meaningful community engagement. 22. To address the recognition, issuance and replacement of documents, the Government, in Law No. 12/2018, established the “e-RCEV” system, facilitating access to civil registry data across the country and streamlining document requests regardless of the applicant’s location. 23. The Special Rapporteur recognizes these developments and stresses the importance of harmonizing efforts and strengthening existing legal frameworks to ensure protection from all drivers of displacement and throughout the displacement cycle.

records.text: Legal and policy framework International and regional frameworks for the protection of internally displaced persons 11. Mozambique is a party to seven of the nine core international treaties, including several optional protocols to those treaties. It has ratified the African Charter on Human and People’s Rights and most regional human rights treaties, including the African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa, known as the Kampala Convention. Mozambique has pledged to: ratify the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and its Optional Protocol as well as the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance; adopt a national action plan on business and human rights; establish a national human rights institution, in accordance with the Paris Principles; organize consultations to align national legislation with international human rights norms and standards in the field of counter‐terrorism; and draft laws on civil society organizations and persons with disabilities.

records.section: Development and extractive industry induced displacement
records.text: 10. While some companies, including Total Energy, the largest private investor in Cabo Delgado Province, have invested in social and environmental programmes for communities affected by their activities, including resettlement and compensation programmes, protection actors the Special Rapporteur spoke to pointed out various protection risks caused by the programmes, including lack of adequate community consultation and participation during relocations, inadequacy of compensation and lack of access to traditional livelihoods and services in relocation areas. The 2022 report commissioned by Total Energy on the socioeconomic, humanitarian and human rights situation in affected areas includes recommendations and an action plan to ensure the compensation of affected persons, the provision of agricultural land and access to fishing areas.

records.section: Internal displacement as a result of armed conflict
records.text: 7. Since 2017, Cabo Delgado Province has been affected by large-scale internal displacement, both within the province and to neighbouring ones, owing to ongoing armed conflict and violence perpetrated by non-State armed groups. The conflict has led to civilian casualties, infrastructure destruction, loss of livelihoods and serious violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. The situation was further exacerbated by the lack of basic infrastructure and services, poverty, unemployment and social inequality owing to pre-existing disparities between the south and the north of the country. In mid-2021, at the Government’s request, the Southern African Development Community deployed a mission to Cabo Delgado. Subsequently, though a bilateral agreement, Rwandan forces were deployed in the province. 8. As of January 2023, the armed conflict in Cabo Delgado Province had claimed 6,500 lives and displaced many people. As of August 2023, there were about 670,000 internally displaced persons in northern Mozambique, while the number of people who had returned to or near their areas of origin stood at over 570,000. According to the Government, that number was in addition to the over 138,000 internally displaced persons in protracted displacement owing to disasters in the central provinces. Over half of the displaced population lives in host communities, including 137,000 people in Pemba City, straining its infrastructure and services, and an estimated 380,000 people are located in 191 displacement sites, many with limited access to safe shelter, water and sanitation. 9. While there was a reduction in the number of attacks by non-State armed groups and an increase in returning populations at the beginning of 2023, violence escalated in December 2023, spreading across various districts and prompting new displacements, including into Nampula Province. In January 2024 alone, there were 23 security incidents, including attacks on villages, clashes with security forces and sightings of non-State armed groups across districts. Between December 2023 and March 2024, escalating violence by non-State armed groups resulted in the forced displacement of around 110,000 newly displaced across Cabo Delgado Province and neighbouring Nampula Province, adding to the over 709,000 persons who have remained displaced since the beginning of the conflict in 2017. The surge in violence has led to numerous human rights violations, including killings, abductions, forced recruitment, sexual violence and infrastructure destruction, exacerbating the already dire humanitarian situation in the region.

records.section: Internal displacement in the context of disasters and the adverse effects of climate change
records.text: 6. Mozambique has been affected by internal displacement as a result of disasters, exacerbated by the adverse effects of climate change, resource extraction projects and armed conflict. Mozambique faces recurrent natural hazards, including droughts, heavy rains, tropical storms and cyclones, their frequency and intensity amplified by the global climate crisis, with major consequences for rural communities. Yearly tropical storms and cyclones have been particularly devastating over the past five years, affecting eight out of 11 provinces and between 750,000 to 1.5 million people annually, resulting in significant damage, including widespread disruptions to the infrastructure and displaced populations. In 2023, Tropical Cyclone Freddy unleased record-breaking winds and rainfall, impacting 1.18 million individuals, displacing nearly 192,000 people and claiming 183 lives, mostly in south-central Mozambique. An estimated 1.2 million people, in particular those reliant on rainfed agriculture, faced heightened vulnerability and food insecurity. Mozambique faces ongoing vulnerability. It is expected that 2.5 million people may be exposed to climatic adversities in the coming rainy/cyclonic season, with dire consequences for communities and infrastructure.

records.text: 4. Mozambique is a country in south-eastern Africa, spanning an area of 799,380 square kilometres, comprising 11 Provinces, with a population of approximately 33.7 million (2021), 51.4 per cent (2023) of which is female. While around one third of the population resides in coastal cities and towns, the majority (62.4 per cent) resides in rural areas. 5. In 2023, Mozambique ranked 183 out of 193 countries on the Human Development Index. Poverty remains a significant challenge: 46 per cent of the population live below the national poverty line, and 63 per cent below the international poverty line, with higher rates observed in rural areas (74 per cent) compared to urban areas (42 per cent). Women, children, persons with disabilities and older persons are disproportionately affected, with 63 per cent of households headed by women; poor; and exposed to food insecurity. Moreover, 48 per cent of women between the ages of 20 to 24 are married before the age of 18.

The Committee invites the State party to submit its combined fifth to seventh periodic reports by 25 November 2024 and to include therein information on the follow-up to the present concluding observations. In the event that a report exceeding the established word limit is submitted, the State party will be asked to shorten the report in accordance with the above-mentioned resolution. records.text: 47. In the light of its general comment No. 24 (2019) on children’s rights in the child justice system, the Committee urges the State party to bring its child justice system fully into line with the Convention and other relevant standards. In particular, the Committee urges the State party: (a) To designate specialized judges for children and ensure that such specialized judges, as well as prosecutors, police officers and other professionals, receive training on the provisions of the Convention; (b) To record the number of children under 18 years of age in prison and other forms of detention separately from the number of persons under 21 years of age, and ensure that the number of children deprived of their liberty is monitored on an ongoing basis; (c) To promote diversion from an early stage in the child justice system, promote the use of non-custodial measures, ensure the availability of measures such as mediation and counselling and roll out a pilot project on community service; (d) To reduce the period of pretrial detention by ensuring that children arrested and deprived of their liberty are promptly brought before a competent authority to examine the legality of the deprivation of liberty or its continuation, in line with article 308 of the Penal Code, provide legal representation for children who are detained and expedite trials involving children; (e) To ensure that detention is used as a last resort and for the shortest period of time possible and that it is reviewed on a regular basis with a view to withdrawing it; (f) To ensure that, in cases where detention is unavoidable, children are not detained together with adults and that detention conditions comply with international standards, including with regard to access to education and health services; (g) To strengthen assistance programmes for children at risk of coming into conflict with the law and provide services for the psychological counselling and social reintegration of children released from prison, including access to education and vocational training.

records.section: Education, including sexual violence in schools
records.text: 41. Taking note of targets 4.1 and 4.2 of the Sustainable Development Goals, the Committee reiterates its previous recommendations (CRC/C/MOZ/CO/2, para. 72) and recommends that the State party: (a) Improve access to and retention in primary and secondary schools and ensure the availability of qualified teachers, transportation to schools, learning and instructional materials and adequate physical infrastructure, including access to clean water and sanitation facilities; (b) Strengthen measures to provide free and compulsory primary education to all children and address the high number of dropouts, particularly among girls, due to pregnancy, child marriage, poverty, fear of sexual abuse and poor sanitary conditions; (c) Improve the quality of education by, inter alia, providing quality training and incentives for teachers, addressing teacher absenteeism and ensuring that curricula and teaching methods are monitored, in cooperation with school councils; (d) Ensure that human rights education, including education on the principles of the Convention, is integrated into the mandatory school curriculum as a matter of priority; (e) Address the sexual abuse and harassment of children, especially girls, by their peers and teachers, by implementing a zero- tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse in schools that includes preventive, protective and support measures, such as counselling, medical and legal assistance, and by strengthening awareness-raising and training of teachers and students; (f) Prioritize and provide adequate resources for the effective enforcement of legislative and administrative provisions, including Ministry of Education instruction No. 5/2016, that prohibit sexual misconduct by teachers and other education personnel and ensure that the sanctions applied are commensurate with the gravity of the offences; (g) Develop and implement strategies to ensure that girls can travel to and from school safely; (h) Allocate adequate resources for the effective implementation and expansion of the integrated development strategy for children in preschool and the bilingual education programme.
